inline.s: The middle grade of rebirth: though unable to shave the head and leave home or to cultivate merit on a grand scale, one should give rise to bodhi-mind and single-mindedly recite Amitābha Buddha,
and according to one's own circumstances do one's utmost to cultivate all wholesome merits

. One observes the fasts and precepts, builds stūpas and Buddha images, gives to monks and nuns, and makes offerings to the Buddha by hanging silk banners, lighting lamps, scattering flowers, and burning incense, dedicating all of this and vowing to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. When such a person is about to die, Amitābha Buddha manifests a transformed body, whose radiance and marks are exactly like those of the true Buddha, and appears before that person together with the great assembly. The person then follows that transformed Buddha and is reborn in that land, dwelling in non-retrogression, with merit and wisdom next to those of the superior grade.
[More or less cultivation of goodness] According to one's own circumstances, do one's utmost to cultivate all wholesome merits.

[The fast and the precepts] Cleansing the impurities of one's own mind is called the “fast”; forbidding the faults of one's own conduct is called the “precepts.” The fast and precepts mean observing the precepts so as to cut off all cravings and faults. [Zeng (
zēng
)] The ancient general term for silk fabrics. [Hanging silk banners] Hanging banners made of silk in a Buddha hall. [Dedication of merit]
Dedicating this merit:
“May this merit adorn the Pure Land of the Buddha
(the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss)
, repaying the four kinds of kindness above and relieving the suffering of the three paths below
(the three evil paths)
, so that all who see or hear give rise to bodhi-mind, and when this retribution body ends, are reborn together in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.”

[The four kinds of kindness] The kindness of parents (the family), the kindness of living beings (society), the kindness of the country (the nation), and the kindness of the Three Jewels (religion). [The Three Jewels] The Buddha Jewel, the Dharma Jewel, and the Saṃgha Jewel. [When this retribution body ends, are reborn together in the Land of Ultimate Bliss] Everyone is reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss at the end of this present life. The “retribution body” spoken of here is the body that is the retribution of karma.
Those of the lowest grade, even if they cannot perform various meritorious deeds,
should give rise to bodhi-mind
and single-mindedly recite Amitābha Buddha
, even for ten recitations
, vowing to be born in that land. Moreover, there are living beings who, on hearing the profound Dharma, rejoice, believe, and delight in it, giving rise to no doubt,
and even for a single thought recite that Buddha

, and with utmost sincerity vow to be born in that land. When such people are about to die, they dream of Amitābha Buddha and likewise attain rebirth, with merit and wisdom next to those of the middle grade.

The lowest grade of rebirth: even if one cannot perform various meritorious deeds, one should give rise to bodhi-mind and single-mindedly recite Amitābha Buddha, even for ten recitations at the point of death, vowing to be born in that land. Moreover, there are living beings who, on hearing the profound Dharma (that is, hearing the Pure Land Dharma-gate), rejoice, believe, and delight in it, giving rise to no doubt, and even for a single thought at the point of death recite that Buddha, and with utmost sincerity vow to be born in that land. When these two kinds of people are about to die, they dream of Amitābha Buddha and likewise attain rebirth, with merit and wisdom next to those of the middle grade.

[Ten recitations at the end of life, and a single thought at the end of life] These are the ten recitations and the single thought at the point of death. Master Ouyi, in his Essential Explanation of the Amitābha Sūtra, taught:
“If faith and vow are firm,
ten recitations or a single thought at the end of life
, one will certainly be reborn.”
He also said:
“Question: If ten recitations and a single thought alike bring rebirth, what need is there of seven days? Answer: Without the seven days' practice done in ordinary times, how could there be
ten recitations or a single thought at the end of life

? Even the lowest of the low, the perverse and evil, are all cases of past causes ripening, and so they meet a good friend at the end of life and, on hearing, give rise to faith and vow. Such a thing happens once in ten thousand; how could one count on luck!”

(Translation: The student again asked: If the ten recitations and the single thought at the end of life can all bring rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, why must one practice to reach single-mindedness? Answer: If one does not practice single-mindedness in ordinary times, where would the ten recitations or the single thought at the end of life come from? Even the lowest of the low, the perverse and evil, all have past causes ripening, and so they meet a good friend at the end of life and, on hearing, give rise to faith and vow. Such a thing happens once in ten thousand; how could one count on luck! The Questions on the Pure Land refutes most thoroughly the mistaken view that “since ten recitations and a single thought alike bring rebirth, what need is there to practice single-mindedness in ordinary times?” People today cannot afford not to read it.) See
An Annotated Explanation of the Amitābha Sūtra

[What need is there of seven days] Why must one practice to reach single-mindedness? The “seven days” here refers to the practice of reaching single-mindedness. In ancient writing, allusions (quotations of classical sources) were favored, and the allusion of the “seven days” comes from the Buddha Speaks of Amitābha Sūtra:

“If a good man or good woman hears the name of Amitābha Buddha and holds it in mind, whether for one day, two days, three days, four days, five days, six days, or seven days, single-mindedly and without confusion, then when that person is about to die, Amitābha Buddha and all the host of holy ones will appear before him. When that person ends his life, his mind will not be inverted, and he will at once be reborn in Amitābha Buddha's Land of Ultimate Bliss.”
The preceding chapter, “Rebirth in the Three Grades,” mainly set forth the ranks of those reborn; this chapter discusses at length the causal practices of rebirth, and so
it is called “the true causes of rebirth.”

[Again, Ānanda, if there are good men or good women who hear this sutra, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, copy and make offerings of it, and day and night without cease seek birth in that land; who give rise to bodhi-mind, uphold all the precepts, and guard and observe them without transgression; who benefit sentient beings and give away all the roots of goodness they create, sharing them with others and bringing them peace and happiness; who are mindful of Amitābha Buddha and of that Buddha-land — such a person, at the end of life, with a countenance like the Buddha's, adorned in all ways, is born in a jeweled land, swiftly hears the Dharma, and never regresses.]

Again, Ānanda, if there are good men or good women who hear this sutra, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, copy it and make offerings of it, and day and night without cease seek birth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss; who give rise to bodhi-mind, uphold all the precepts, and guard and observe them without transgression; who benefit sentient beings and give away all the good they do, sharing it with them and bringing them peace and happiness; who are mindful of Amitābha Buddha and of the Land of Ultimate Bliss — such a person, at the end of life, with a countenance like the Buddha's, adorned in all ways, is born in a jeweled land, swiftly hears the Dharma, and never regresses.

[The precepts] To forbid the non-precepts and to guard against evil. The precepts instituted by the Buddha include the five precepts, the eight precepts, the śrāmaṇera precepts, and the full precepts, among others. [Benefit] To bring profit to others. [A countenance like the Buddha's] One's countenance is like the Buddha's — a body of true golden hue with the thirty-two marks.

[Again, Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who wish to be born in that land, though they cannot greatly exert themselves in dhyāna and meditation, nor fully uphold the sutras and precepts, they should still do good. That is: first, not to kill; second, not to steal; third, not to commit sexual misconduct; fourth, not to speak falsely; fifth, not to speak with idle or suggestive words; sixth, not to speak harshly; seventh, not to speak divisively; eighth, not to be greedy; ninth, not to be angry; tenth, not to be deluded. Thus, pondering day and night on the Land of Ultimate Bliss, on Amitābha Buddha, on his many virtues and many adornments, they take refuge with all their hearts, bow, and make offerings. When such a person is about to die, unalarmed and unafraid, with a mind that is not inverted, that person at once attains rebirth in that Buddha's land.]

Again, Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who wish to be born in that land, though they cannot greatly exert themselves in dhyāna and meditation, nor fully uphold the sutras and precepts, they should still do good. That is: first, not to kill; second, not to steal; third, not to commit sexual misconduct; fourth, not to speak falsely (not to speak words that are untrue); fifth, not to speak with idle or suggestive words (not to speak filthy words, meaningless words, or words carrying lustful intent); sixth, not to speak harshly (not to revile or mock others with venomous words); seventh, not to speak divisively (not to stir up trouble and set others at odds); eighth, not to be greedy; ninth, not to be angry; tenth, not to be deluded (not to be foolish). Thus, pondering day and night on the many virtues and many adornments of the Land of Ultimate Bliss and of Amitābha Buddha, they take refuge with all their hearts, bow, and make offerings. When such a person is about to die, unalarmed and unafraid, with a mind that is not inverted, that person at once attains rebirth in that Buddha's land.

[If one has many affairs, cannot leave the household, and has no leisure to cultivate the fasts and precepts on a grand scale, one should keep the mind single and pure. When one has leisure, one should set the body and mind upright, cut off desires and cast away worries, and with a compassionate mind press forward diligently. One should not give way to anger or envy, nor be greedy and insatiable
tiè
or stingy
qiān
. One should not waver midway, and should not harbor doubt.]

If one's affairs are many and one cannot leave the household, and one has no leisure to cultivate the fasts and precepts on a grand scale, one should keep the mind single and pure. But when one has leisure, one should set the body and mind upright, cut off desires and cast away worries, and with a compassionate mind press forward diligently. One should not give way to anger or envy, and should not be greedy or stingy. Toward the Pure Land Dharma-gate one should not waver midway, and should not harbor doubt.
[No leisure] To have no time; to be unable to manage it. [Greedy and insatiable (tiè)] Insatiably greedy. [Wavering midway] One's faith is not firm, believing first and doubting later.

[One should be filial and compliant, utterly sincere and loyal. One should believe that the words of the Buddha's sutras are profound, and believe that doing good brings blessing. One should receive, uphold, and practice teachings such as these without loss. Pondering and planning deeply, one should wish to attain liberation. Day and night one should constantly be mindful, vowing and wishing to be reborn in Amitābha Buddha's pure Buddha-land. Those who do not let this break off for ten days and nights, or even for one day and one night, will all, at the end of life, be reborn in that land and practice the bodhisattva path.]

One should be filial and compliant, utterly sincere and loyal. One should believe that the words of the Buddha's sutras are profound, and believe that doing good brings blessing. One should receive, uphold, and practice teachings such as these without loss. Pondering and planning deeply, one should wish to attain liberation (to transcend the round of rebirth). Day and night one should constantly be mindful, vowing and wishing to be reborn in Amitābha Buddha's pure Buddha-land. Those who do not let this break off for ten days and nights, or even for one day and one night, will all, at the end of life, be reborn in that land and practice the bodhisattva path.

[All those who are reborn all attain avaivartika, all are complete in a body of true golden hue and the thirty-two marks, and all shall become Buddhas. In whatever direction and whatever Buddha-land they wish to become Buddhas, it is according to the wish of their minds. According to their diligence, whether they seek the Way early or late and never rest, they will surely attain it and will not lose what they have vowed.]

All those who are reborn all attain the stage of no regression, all are complete in a body of true golden hue and the thirty-two marks, and all shall become Buddhas. In whatever direction and whatever Buddha-land they wish to become Buddhas, it is entirely according to the wish of their minds. According to their diligence, whether they seek the Way early or late and never rest, they will surely become Buddhas and will not lose what they have vowed.

[Ānanda, for the sake of this benefit of meaning and profit, the Tathāgatas of countless, immeasurable, inconceivable, incomparable, boundless worlds all together praise the merits of Amitābha Buddha.]

Ānanda, for the sake of this benefit of meaning and profit, the Tathāgatas of countless, immeasurable, inconceivable, incomparable, boundless worlds all together praise all the merits of Amitābha Buddha.
[Meaning and profit] Meaning is what is fair and fitting in principle and conduct; profit is benefit.

blocks.text: 26. Journeying to Worship in the Land of Ultimate Bliss

inline.s: The next passage explains how the bodhisattvas of the worlds of the ten directions go to the Land of Ultimate Bliss to worship, make offerings, and hear the Dharma.

[Again, Ānanda, the bodhisattvas of the worlds of the ten directions, wishing to behold and worship Amitābha Buddha in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, each take incense, flowers, banners, and jeweled canopies and go to where that Buddha is. Reverently making offerings, they hear and receive the sutras and Dharma, proclaim and spread the teaching, and praise the merits and adornments of that Buddha-land.]

Again, Ānanda, the bodhisattvas of the worlds of the ten directions, wishing to behold and worship Amitābha Buddha in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, each take incense, flowers, banners, and jeweled canopies and go to where Amitābha Buddha is. Reverently making offerings, they hear, receive, and uphold the sutras and Dharma spoken by Amitābha Buddha, and then proclaim and spread his teaching throughout the worlds of the ten directions, praising the merits and adornments of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
[At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
Then the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
In the Buddha-lands of the east, countless as the sands of the Ganges, bodhisattvas as numerous as those sands journey to worship Immeasurable Life.
South, west, north, and the four intermediate directions
(south, west, north, and southeast, southwest, northwest, northeast)
— above and below are likewise so
(the realms above and below are also like this)
, and all with
(all with)
a reverent mind present rare and wonderful offerings
(making all kinds of rare and wonderful offerings to Amitābha Buddha)
(These bodhisattvas)
freely send forth harmonious and elegant sounds, singing in praise of the Most Supreme Honored One
(singing in praise of Amitābha Buddha)
, having fully penetrated the spiritual powers and wisdom
(the spiritual powers and wisdom that are thoroughly mastered)
, and roam freely into the profound Dharma-gate.

[The Most Supreme Honored One] The highest among all honored ones; this is an honorific title for the Buddha. [Roam freely into the profound Dharma-gate] The bodhisattvas, in singing the praises of Amitābha Buddha, exhaust the very source of the true nature of all dharmas, freely and without hindrance roaming through this exceedingly profound Dharma-gate.
Hearing the Buddha's name of holy virtue, they find peace and gain great benefit; among all kinds of offerings, they cultivate diligently without weariness or slackness.
Beholding that supreme land
(the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss)
, so subtle and wondrous as to defy thought, adorned everywhere with merit, beyond compare among all Buddha-lands, they therefore give rise to the unsurpassed mind and vow swiftly to attain bodhi.
The above is the offering, singing, praising, and resolve of the bodhisattvas from the worlds of the ten directions who journey to worship Amitābha Buddha.
Then the Honored One of Immeasurable Life
(at this time, Amitābha Buddha)

, smiling, reveals his golden countenance. Radiance issues from his mouth, illuminating the lands of the ten directions everywhere; the light returns and circles the Buddha, and entering from the crown of his head after three circuits.
Seeing this light, the bodhisattvas at once realize the stage of non-regression, and the whole assembly of the great gathering
(at this time, the whole great assembly present)
rejoiced together, congratulating one another.
What follows is the teaching given by Amitābha Buddha.
The Buddha's words resound like thunder in the Brahmā voice
(Amitābha Buddha teaches in the pure and subtle Brahmā voice; like thunder, it suddenly awakens the great assembly)
, and in the eight tones he pours forth the wondrous sound.

[The Brahmā voice] The pure voice produced by the Great Brahmā King; the Buddha's voice is likewise so, and therefore among the thirty-two marks there is the mark of the Brahmā voice: “the Brahmā voice, pure and far-reaching.” The Lotus Sūtra says:
“The Brahmā voice is subtle and wondrous, delighting all who hear it.”

[The eight tones] The eight kinds of voice unique to the Buddha. First, the supremely excellent tone: all voices of the world and beyond it cannot compare with it. Second, the soft and gentle tone: the Buddha's voice is soft, and those who hear it rejoice. Third, the harmonious tone: it can harmonize the minds of living beings and cause them to rid themselves of affliction. Fourth, the infallible tone: the Buddha's wisdom is perfect and clear, and all who hear the sounds he utters gain right view. Fifth, the tone that is not feminine: the Buddha's voice is complete in the four fearlessnesses, convincing those who hear it. Sixth, the honored and wise tone: the Buddha's voice can cause living beings to give rise to reverence and open their wisdom. Seventh, the deep and far-reaching tone: the Buddha's voice is not loud when heard near, nor small when heard far, and nothing is beyond its reach (however far the place, there is none it does not reach). Eighth, the inexhaustible tone: the Buddha's voice flows on endlessly, its sound never ceasing.
The true ones who come from the ten directions
(the bodhisattvas come from the worlds of the ten directions)
, I know all their vows
(I fully know their supreme great vows)
, their resolve to seek and adorn a pure land
(their resolve to embrace and create a pure and adorned Buddha-land)
, and for them the prediction will be given that they shall become Buddhas.
[The prediction]
To receive from the Buddha the assurance that one will certainly become a Buddha in the future.
(They)
awaken to all dharmas as dream, illusion, and echo
(entering the true nature of all dharmas, awakening to and penetrating the fact that all dharmas are ultimately empty, nonexistent, and unattainable)
, fulfill all their wondrous vows
(fulfilling their supreme great vows)
, and shall surely accomplish such a land
(they will certainly build such a Buddha-land)
(They)
know that lands are like reflections and images
(knowing that Buddha-lands are likewise illusory appearances)
, constantly give rise to the mind of vast vows, and fulfill the bodhisattva path to the end
(thoroughly and perfectly practicing the bodhisattva path)
, complete in all the roots of merit, cultivating the supreme bodhi practice
(cultivating the supreme bodhi practice)
, and for them the prediction will be given that they shall become Buddhas.

[Knowing that lands are like reflections and images] Knowing that Buddha-lands are also like the reflections and images of things: though born from a real substance, they have no real nature. This speaks of how the bodhisattvas enter the true nature of all dharmas and know that Buddha-lands too are illusory appearances. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

“Perfect enlightenment shines everywhere, still and quiescent without duality, and within it the Buddha-worlds of hundreds of thousands of millions of asaṃkhyeyas of unutterable Ganges-sands are like flowers in the sky, rising and ceasing in confusion.”
(For annotations see
A Detailed Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment
(They)
penetrate the nature of all dharmas
(penetrating the true nature of all dharmas)
, all is empty and without self
(all the myriad phenomena are illusory appearances without real substance. For details see
The True Nature of All Dharmas
, and they seek solely the pure Buddha-land
(seeking solely to embrace and create their own Buddha-land)
, and shall surely accomplish such a land
(they will certainly build such a Buddha-land)
(They)

hearing the Dharma, delight in receiving and practicing it, and attain the pure place; before the Honored One of Immeasurable Life they shall receive the prediction and accomplish equal enlightenment.

[They shall, before the Honored One of Immeasurable Life, receive the prediction and accomplish equal enlightenment] They shall receive the prediction of Buddhahood from Amitābha Buddha. The “equal enlightenment” here is the abbreviated form of “true equal and perfect enlightenment.”
The next passage explains how the bodhisattvas of the assembly, wishing to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, at once attain the stage of non-regression.
The boundless and supreme land
(the Land of Ultimate Bliss is supremely wondrous, without limit or measure, surpassing all the Buddha-lands of the ten directions)
, by the power of that Buddha's original vows
(precisely through the power of Amitābha Buddha's supreme original vows)
: hearing the name and wishing to be reborn
(the bodhisattvas, hearing the name of Amitābha Buddha, wish to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss)
, they attain non-regression of themselves
(having arrived there, they themselves attain the stage of non-regression)
The next passage explains how
the bodhisattvas of the assembly
give rise to the most vast of vows, wishing to
build a Buddha-land like the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, and to save all living beings from the six paths of rebirth, bringing them to be reborn in their own Buddha-lands.
Bodhisattvas give rise to the supreme vow
(the bodhisattvas give rise to the most vast of vows)
, vowing that their own lands be without difference
(vowing that the Buddha-land they will build in the future be like the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss)
, and with universal mindfulness
(equal great compassion)
save all
(saving all living beings)
(causing them)
each to give rise to bodhi-mind, to abandon the body of rebirth, and all to reach the other shore
(all to be reborn in those Buddha-lands of the bodhisattvas, which are like the Land of Ultimate Bliss — this is the other shore where there is no rebirth in birth and death)
[Vowing that their own lands be without difference] Vowing that the Buddha-land one builds be like the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
This is just as with Prince Ajātaśatru and the five hundred great elders earlier in the text, who vowed in their minds: when we become Buddhas, may it be just like Amitābha Buddha.
The Buddha Speaks of the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life (Wei translation) says:
“Bodhisattvas give rise to the supreme vow, vowing that their own lands be without difference; with universal mindfulness they save all, and their fame shines throughout the ten directions.”

In the sutra text, “with universal mindfulness they save all” clearly means that the bodhisattvas who give rise to the supreme vow wish to save all living beings and bring them to the Buddha-lands they will build in the future, which are like the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. [Abandon the body of rebirth] “That” refers to the living beings whom these bodhisattvas wish to save, not to the bodhisattvas themselves. For the bodhisattvas who can come from the Buddha-lands of the ten directions to worship and make offerings to Amitābha Buddha no longer have a body of rebirth.
The next passage explains how the bodhisattvas of the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss fly and transform themselves to the Buddha-lands of the ten directions to make offerings to all Buddhas.

[The Buddha said to Ānanda: The bodhisattvas of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, by the awesome spiritual power of the Buddha, within the time of a single meal go again to the boundless pure lands of the ten directions to make offerings to all Buddhas. Flowers, incense, banners, and canopies — the implements of offering — arrive as soon as they are thought of and all appear in their hands. Rare, wonderful, and extraordinary, such as the world does not possess, they are presented to all the Buddhas and to the assemblies of bodhisattvas.]

The Buddha said to Ānanda: The bodhisattvas of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, by the awesome spiritual power of the Buddha, within the time of a single meal go to the boundless pure lands of the ten directions to make offerings to all Buddhas. Flowers, precious incense, banners, and canopies — the implements of offering — arrive as soon as they are thought of and all appear in their hands. Rare, wonderful, and extraordinary, such as the world does not possess, they are used to make offerings to all the Buddhas of the boundless pure lands of the ten directions, and to the assemblies of bodhisattvas.
[The time of a single meal] The time it takes to eat one meal. In the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra,
Fascicle 347,

the Chapter of Entrustment, the lengths of time are divided in order into: a day and a night, a day, half a day, one hour (equivalent to two hours today), the time of a meal, a moment, a short while, and the space of a breath.

[The flowers they scatter at once join together in the sky into a single flower. The flowers all face downward, forming a perfect circle at the rim, and transform into a flower canopy. With hundreds of thousands of light-hues, each hue giving off a different fragrance, the fragrance pervades everywhere. The smallest of the canopies fills ten yojanas, and doubling in this way, they extend to cover the great trichiliocosm. Following one another in order, they transform and disappear. If new flowers are not scattered again, the flowers scattered before never fall. In the sky they together play celestial music, and with subtle and wondrous sounds sing in praise of the Buddha's virtues.]

The fresh flowers they scatter at once join together in the sky into a single flower. The flowers all face downward, forming a perfect circle at the rim, and transform into a flower canopy, giving forth hundreds of thousands of light-hues. Each hue of light also sends out a different fragrance, pervading the four directions. The smallest of the canopies is fully ten yojanas across, and doubling in this way, they extend to cover the great trichiliocosm. Following one another in order, they transform and disappear. If new flowers are not scattered again, the fresh flowers scattered before hang in the sky all the while. In the sky they together play celestial music, and with subtle and wondrous sounds sing in praise of the Buddha's virtues.

[After a moment, they return to their own land and all assemble in the seven-jeweled lecture hall. Amitābha Buddha widely proclaims the great teaching for them and expounds the wondrous Dharma. None is other than joyful, their minds opened to understanding and attaining the Way.]

After a moment, they return to the Land of Ultimate Bliss and all assemble in the seven-jeweled lecture hall. Amitābha Buddha then widely proclaims the great teaching for them and expounds the wondrous Dharma thoroughly. None in the assembly is other than joyful, their minds opened to understanding and attaining the Way.

[At once a fragrant breeze blows on the seven-jeweled trees, giving forth the five tones. Countless wondrous flowers scatter in all directions with the wind, making offerings of themselves, and so it continues without cease. All the celestial beings carry
jī

hundreds of thousands of flowers, fragrances, and ten thousand kinds of music and dance, making offerings to that Buddha and to the assemblies of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas. Coming and going one after another, they are joyous and happy. All of this is through the added majesty of Amitābha Buddha's original vows, and because they once made offerings to the Tathāgatas, their roots of goodness continue without diminution, because they cultivated well, because they embraced well, because they accomplished well.]

At once a fragrant breeze blows on the seven-jeweled trees, giving forth the five tones (gōng, shāng, jué, zhǐ, yǔ). Countless wondrous flowers scatter in all directions with the wind, making offerings of themselves, and so it continues without cease. All the celestial beings of the heavens carry hundreds of thousands of kinds of fresh flowers and precious incense, and ten thousand kinds of music and dance (music and dancing), making offerings to Amitābha Buddha and to the great assemblies of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas. Coming and going one after another, they are joyous and happy. All of this is through the added majesty of Amitābha Buddha's original vows, and because they (all the celestial beings of the heavens) once made offerings to the Tathāgatas, their roots of goodness continue without diminution, because they cultivated well, because they embraced well, because they accomplished well.
[Carry (
jī
)] To carry along.

[The Buddha told Ānanda: All the bodhisattvas in that Buddha's land can see and hear clearly throughout the eight directions, above and below, and the affairs of past, future, and present. The celestial beings and people, and even the flying insects and crawling creatures — the good or evil of their minds, what their mouths wish to say, when they will be liberated, when they will attain the Way and be reborn — all of this they know in advance.]

The Buddha told Ānanda: All the bodhisattvas of the Land of Ultimate Bliss can see and hear clearly throughout the eight directions, above and below (the ten directions), and the affairs of past, future, and present. As for beings from the celestial beings and people above down to the flying insects and crawling creatures — the good or evil of their minds, what their mouths wish to say, when they will be liberated, when they will attain the Way and be reborn — they all know it in advance.

[Further, the śrāvakas in that Buddha's land have a bodily radiance of one fathom, while the radiance of the bodhisattvas illumines a hundred yojanas. There are two bodhisattvas, foremost and most honored, whose awesome spiritual radiance illumines the great trichiliocosm everywhere.]

Further, in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the śrāvakas have a bodily radiance of eight feet, while the radiance of the bodhisattvas illumines a hundred yojanas. There are two bodhisattvas, foremost and most honored, whose awesome spiritual radiance illumines the great trichiliocosm everywhere.
[Fathom] An ancient unit of length; one fathom equals eight feet.
[Ānanda said to the Buddha: What are the names of those two bodhisattvas?]
Ānanda said to the Buddha: What are the names of these two bodhisattvas?

[The Buddha said: One is named Avalokiteśvara, and one is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta. These two bodhisattvas, in the Sahā world, practiced the bodhisattva path and were reborn in that land, and they constantly stand to the left and right of Amitābha Buddha. Wishing to go to the places of the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions, they arrive according to their minds. They now dwell in this world, bringing great benefit and joy. If good men or good women in the world meet with urgent peril and terror, let them simply take refuge in Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, and there is none who is not freed.]

The Buddha said: One is named Avalokiteśvara, and one is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta. These two bodhisattvas practiced the bodhisattva path in the Sahā world and were reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, and they constantly stand to the left and right of Amitābha Buddha. When they wish to go to the places of the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions, they arrive according to their minds. They now dwell in this Sahā world, bringing great benefit and joy (rescuing from peril, relieving suffering, and giving happiness) to living beings. If good men or good women in the world meet with urgent peril and terror, let them simply take refuge in Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, and there is none who is not freed.

[Again, Ānanda, all the bodhisattvas in that Buddha's land, present and future, shall all ultimately reach the stage of one lifetime from Buddhahood. Only those who have made great vows are excepted: entering the realm of birth and death to save living beings, they give the lion's roar. Putting on
huàn, to put on
the great armor
zhòu, helmet

, they adorn themselves with the merit of their vast vows. Though born in the evil world of the five turbidities and manifesting in the same manner as its beings, they do not fall into the evil paths right up to the time they become Buddhas; and wherever they are born, they always know their past lives.]

Again, Ānanda, all the bodhisattvas in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, present and future, shall ultimately reach the stage of one lifetime from Buddhahood (equal enlightenment bodhisattvas). Only those bodhisattvas who have made supreme vast vows are excepted: they willingly take birth in impure lands that have birth and death, to save the living beings there. Like the Buddha, they expound the sutras and teach the Dharma (giving the lion's roar), spreading the Pure Land Dharma-gate and saving living beings, bringing them to rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. Clad in the great armor with which they adorn themselves by the merit of their vast vows, though born in the evil world of the five turbidities and manifesting in the same manner as its beings, they do not fall into the evil paths right up to the time they become Buddhas; and wherever they are born, they are free of the obscurity of the intervening skandha, knowing everything of their past lives.

[Entering the realm of birth and death] To take birth in impure lands that have the round of birth and death. [The lion's roar] When the Buddha expounds the Dharma amid the great assembly, fearing no crowd of false teachers or heterodox learning, he is like a lion roaring and overawing the hundred beasts. [Giving the lion's roar] To expound the sutras and teach the Dharma like the Buddha. [The obscurity of the intervening skandha] To forget as soon as one is reborn into another life.

[Amitābha Buddha wishes to save and liberate all kinds of living beings in the worlds of the ten directions, causing them all to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss and attain the path of nirvāṇa, and causing them all to become Buddhas. Once they have become Buddhas, they in turn teach and save one another throughout the worlds of the ten directions. Thus passing it on from one to another, they cannot be counted again.]

Amitābha Buddha wishes to save and liberate all kinds of living beings in the worlds of the ten directions, causing them all to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss (because this is the easiest way to transcend birth and death and escape the round of rebirth), to attain the path to Buddhahood, and to become Buddhas, all of them. After they have become Buddhas, they in turn teach the Pure Land Dharma-gate throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and in turn save the living beings there, bringing them to rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. The living beings thus taught and saved from one to another cannot be counted.
[Nirvāṇa (
huán
)] That is, nirvāṇa. [Attaining the path of nirvāṇa] Gaining the path to Buddhahood.

All kinds of living beings in the worlds of the ten directions, having been reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, will all reach the stage of one lifetime from Buddhahood (equal enlightenment bodhisattvas), and then go to the worlds of the ten directions to become Buddhas (accomplishing the eight aspects of the path to Buddhahood).

[Amitābha Buddha wishes to save and liberate all kinds of living beings in the worlds of the ten directions, causing them all to be reborn in his land (the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss)] This is Amitābha Buddha's immeasurable compassion. It is precisely because Amitābha Buddha, while in the causal stage, endured every hardship and passed through immeasurable, inconceivable, countless kalpas that he built the incomparably supreme Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, and thus there is the Pure Land Dharma-gate. When living beings of the evil world of the five turbidities practice the Pure Land Dharma-gate, they need only recite Amitābha Buddha continuously for ten thoughts at the end of life to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss and transcend birth and death and escape the round of rebirth (for details see
The Conditions for Rebirth

). Other Dharma-gates, by contrast, require cutting off affliction entirely (the delusions of view and thought) before one can transcend birth and death and escape the round of rebirth. Comparing the difficulty of the two, the former is like sailing before the wind with raised sails, while the latter is like an ant climbing a high mountain. Therefore it is said:
“In the Dharma-ending age, of hundreds of millions upon hundreds of millions who practice, scarcely one attains the Way; only by relying on Buddha-recitation does one escape birth and death.”

[Other Dharma-gates, by contrast, require cutting off affliction entirely (the delusions of view and thought) before one can transcend birth and death and escape the round of rebirth] Take Chan practice as an example. The process of cutting off affliction entirely is: ten thousand thoughts returning to one (only a single thought remaining in the mind, such as a huatou), one returning to nothing (not a single thought arising), clearly seeing one's own nature (thoroughly beholding the original nature), and then doing the work of guarding and sustaining it until the delusions of view and thought are utterly cut off. Only then can one transcend birth and death and escape the round of rebirth. And its very first and easiest stage, “ten thousand thoughts returning to one,” is equivalent to single-mindedness in the Pure Land Dharma-gate. In the Pure Land Dharma-gate, one need only reach single-mindedness to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss in the upper grade, one hundred percent, and thus transcend birth and death and escape the round of rebirth. Therefore, of those who practice Chan to transcend birth and death, scarcely one in a hundred million succeeds, while of those who recite the Buddha's name, ten thousand practice and ten thousand go. From this we can know how vast and profound Amitābha Buddha's grace and virtue are, and how rare and precious the Pure Land Dharma-gate is. Hence the Buddha said:
“That you
(Ānanda)

have now asked this question surpasses in merit by hundreds of thousands of millions of times the offering of a world of arhats and pratyekabuddhas, and the giving of alms to the celestial beings and people and the flying and crawling creatures of many kalpas. Why is that? Because the celestial beings and people and all living beings with consciousness of the future
will all attain liberation through your question
[One who is single-minded is reborn in the upper grade]
Bodhisattva Jue Ming Miao Xing said:

“When one is mindful in this way, affliction and the dust of toil are neither cut off nor bound — there is only one mind. One must attain single-mindedness before one can be said to be holding the name, before one can be said to be single-minded and undisturbed; then the work of the pure karma is accomplished, and one goes straight to the upper grade.”
(For details see
An Annotated Edition of The Definitive Guide to the West

[Ten thousand practice, ten thousand go] The “practice” here means true practice done in earnest, with correct method and arduous effort. Those who practice blindly and recklessly, or who shrink back out of fear of difficulty and grow lazy, are not included.

[The śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and all kinds of living beings of the worlds of the ten directions who are born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, attain the path of nirvāṇa, and are to become Buddhas cannot be counted. Yet in that Buddha's land it is always as it was, without increase. Why is that? It is like the great ocean, king among the waters: as all the waters flow and enter the sea, does the water of the great ocean increase?]

The śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and all kinds of living beings of the worlds of the ten directions who are reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss and attain the path to Buddhahood, who are to become Buddhas, cannot be counted. Yet the Land of Ultimate Bliss remains just as it was, with no increase in the number of its people. Why is that? It is like the great ocean, king among the waters: as all the waters flow and enter the sea, can the water of the great ocean be seen to increase?

[Always as it was, without increase] Although the living beings of the worlds of the ten directions who are reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss cannot be counted, the Land of Ultimate Bliss remains just as it was. This is like ten thousand rivers flowing into the great ocean, whose waters are not seen to increase because of it. This describes how the Land of Ultimate Bliss is incomparably vast and its people exceedingly numerous. In “Immeasurable Lifespans and Multitudes, Chapter Thirteen,” the Buddha says:

“Among my disciples, Mahāmaudgalyāyana is foremost in spiritual powers: the number of all the living beings among the stars in the great trichiliocosm — he knows them all in a single day and night. Suppose all the living beings of the ten directions became pratyekabuddhas, and each pratyekabuddha lived for a trillion years with spiritual powers like Mahāmaudgalyāyana's. Exhausting their lifespans and their powers of wisdom to calculate together the number of śrāvakas in that Buddha's assembly, they would not reach even one part in ten million.”

[In the eight directions, above and below, Buddha-lands are countless. The Land of Ultimate Bliss is lasting and vast, bright and beautiful, happy and joyful, and supremely unsurpassed. This is what his seeking of the Way, his vows, and his accumulated virtue accomplished when he was a bodhisattva. Amitābha Buddha's grace and giving extend through the eight directions, above and below, endlessly without limit, deep and vast beyond measure, beyond all telling.]

In the eight directions, above and below (the ten directions), Buddha-lands are countless. Amitābha Buddha's Land of Ultimate Bliss is lasting and vast, bright and beautiful, happy and joyful, and supremely unsurpassed. All of this is what his seeking of the Way, his vows, and his accumulated merit accomplished when he was a bodhisattva. Amitābha Buddha's grace and giving extend through the eight directions, above and below (the ten directions), endlessly without limit, deep and vast beyond measure, beyond all telling.

[Again, Ānanda, all the bodhisattvas in that Buddha's land are complete in dhyāna, wisdom, spiritual powers, and majestic virtue without exception. The secret store of all Buddhas they understand thoroughly and clearly. They tame and subdue the faculties, and their bodies and minds are gentle and pliant. Deeply entering right wisdom, they have no remaining habits. Following what the Buddha practiced, they follow the seven factors of enlightenment and the noble path.]

Again, Ānanda, all the bodhisattvas in the Land of Ultimate Bliss are complete in dhyāna, wisdom, spiritual powers, and majestic virtue without exception. As for the original nature (the secret store of all Buddhas), they understand it thoroughly and clearly. They tame and subdue the faculties, and their bodies (their conduct) and minds are gentle and pliant. Deeply entering right wisdom, they have no more habitual tendencies. Following what the Buddha taught, they cultivate and uphold the seven factors of enlightenment and the noble eightfold path.

[Gentle and pliant] Body (conduct) and mind are soft and yielding in accord with the Way, not hard and unyielding and difficult to transform. [Remaining habits] After affliction has been cut off, the residual habitual tendencies; or simply called habitual tendencies. [The seven factors of enlightenment] That is, the seven limbs of enlightenment, also called the seven factors of bodhi, the seven branches of enlightenment, and the seven equal-enlightenment branches: the seven kinds of awakening manifested by the five roots and five powers. First, the enlightenment factor of discrimination of dharmas: using wisdom to discern the true from the false in dharmas. Second, the enlightenment factor of diligence: with a courageous mind, vigorously practicing the right Dharma. Third, the enlightenment factor of joy: the mind attaining the good Dharma and giving rise to joy. Fourth, the enlightenment factor of ease: ridding body and mind of coarse and heavy affliction and gaining lightness and peace. Fifth, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness: constantly contemplating the right Dharma, so that concentration and wisdom are balanced. Sixth, the enlightenment factor of concentration: the mind resting on a single object without distraction. Seventh, the enlightenment factor of equanimity: casting off all false dharmas and vigorously practicing the right Dharma. [The five roots] The root of faith, the root of diligence, the root of mindfulness, the root of concentration, and the root of wisdom. Because these five dharmas are the roots from which the noble path arises, they are called the “five roots.” [The five powers] When the five roots become firm and generate strength, they are called the “five powers”: the power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. The power of faith is the growth of the root of faith, able to destroy all wrong faith; the power of diligence is the growth of the root of diligence, able to destroy the laziness of body and mind; the power of mindfulness is the growth of the root of mindfulness, able to destroy all wrong thoughts; the power of concentration is the growth of the root of concentration, able to destroy all scattered thinking; the power of wisdom is the growth of the root of wisdom, able to destroy all the delusions of the three realms.

[The noble eightfold path] Also called the eight right paths: the eight path-dharmas of the noble ones. First, right view: correct knowledge and insight. Second, right thought: correct thinking. Third, right speech: proper speech. Fourth, right action: proper conduct. Fifth, right livelihood: a proper profession or way of life. Sixth, right effort: proper endeavor. Seventh, right mindfulness: correct recollection. Eighth, right concentration: correct dhyāna.

[Cultivating the five eyes, they illumine the true and penetrate the mundane. The physical eye discerns, the celestial eye sees everywhere, the Dharma eye is pure, the wisdom eye beholds the true, and the Buddha eye is complete, awakening to the nature of all dharmas.]

They cultivate the five eyes, illumining the true and penetrating the mundane. The physical eye discerns (it can skillfully distinguish the characteristics of all dharmas); the celestial eye sees everywhere (near and far, obstructed and unobstructed, by day and by night, all without hindrance); the Dharma eye is pure (it thoroughly understands all Dharma-gates of the world and beyond it); the wisdom eye beholds the true (it sees through false appearances and recognizes true emptiness); the Buddha eye is complete (nothing is unknown to it, nothing is unseen by it), awakening to the true nature of all dharmas.
The Buddha Speaks of the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life (Wei translation) says:

“The physical eye is clear and pure, nothing it does not distinguish; the celestial eye sees everywhere, immeasurable and unlimited; the Dharma eye observes, penetrating all paths to the end; the wisdom eye beholds the true and can cross to the other shore; the Buddha eye is complete, awakening to the nature of all dharmas.”

[The five eyes] The physical eye, the celestial eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye. The physical eye is the eye of ordinary beings of flesh: meeting darkness or meeting obstruction, it cannot see. The celestial eye is the eye of celestial beings: near and far, obstructed, by day and by night, it can see all. The wisdom eye is the eye of the śrāvakas: it can see through false appearances and recognize true emptiness. The Dharma eye is the eye of the bodhisattvas: it can thoroughly understand all Dharma-gates of the world and beyond it. The Buddha eye is the eye of the Tathāgata: having the Buddha eye, one also possesses the four preceding eyes, and nothing is unknown to one, nothing is unseen; amid all dharmas, the Buddha eye constantly illumines.

[Illumining the true and penetrating the mundane] To illumine the true nature of all dharmas and to penetrate all myriad phenomena. By illumining the true, one's own practice is perfected and reaches the ultimate; by penetrating the mundane, one sets forth teachings according to capacity and saves immeasurable living beings. The Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
“One can skillfully distinguish the characteristics of all dharmas, yet is unmoved in the supreme meaning.”
[The supreme meaning] That is, the supreme meaning truth, the highest, most perfect, and ultimate truth. The true nature of all dharmas is the supreme meaning truth. The Buddha says:

“All dharmas are false and deceptive; where they cease, that is called the real, called the true nature, called the Dharma realm, called ultimate wisdom, called the supreme meaning truth, called the supreme meaning emptiness.”
(The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra)

[Complete in eloquence, free and unobstructed. They skillfully understand the world and its boundless skillful means. What they say is sincere and true, deeply entering the flavor of the meaning. They save all living beings, expounding the right Dharma. Without characteristics, without contrivance, without bondage, without liberation. Without all discriminations, far removed from inversion. In all that they enjoy, they take no attachment.]

These bodhisattvas are complete in all eloquence, free and unobstructed. They skillfully understand the boundless skillful means of the world. What they say is sincere and true (sincere and truthful), deeply entering the flavor of the meaning. They save all living beings, expounding the right Dharma. Without characteristics, without contrivance, without bondage, without liberation. Without all discriminations, far removed from inversion. In all that they enjoy, they take no attachment (they are attached to no appearance at all).
[Complete in eloquence] Holding all kinds of eloquence, that is, complete in all eloquence. The Buddha Speaks of the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life (Wei translation) says:
“Complete in all eloquence.”

[Skillful means] The devices, methods, or language adopted in order to guide and teach living beings. The so-called “skillful means” is spoken in contrast to the real (the true nature of all dharmas). [Without characteristics, without contrivance] That is, as the Diamond Sūtra says:

“All kinds of living beings — whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether with form or without form; whether with thought, without thought, or neither with nor without thought — I cause them all to enter the remainderless nirvāṇa and be liberated
(I must bring them all to Buddhahood)
. And thus I liberate immeasurable, countless, boundless living beings
(having thus liberated immeasurable, countless, boundless living beings and brought them to Buddhahood)
, yet in truth there are no living beings who attain liberation
(and yet in truth there is no such thing as a living being who is saved and becomes a Buddha)
(For annotations see
A Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sūtra
[Without characteristics] That is, not attached to appearances. The Diamond Sūtra says:
“Whatever has characteristics is all false and deceptive.”
(For annotations see
A Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sūtra

) [Attached to appearances] Taking appearances as real, so that there is love and hate, grasping and rejecting, and one is entangled by them. [Without bondage, without liberation] There is neither bondage nor liberation. The world takes ignorance and affliction as bondage, and the cutting off of delusion and the revealing of the true as liberation. But these bodhisattvas have awakened to the nature of dharmas and clearly understand that the essence of the true and the false is one; entering the Dharma-gate of non-duality, they are therefore without bondage and without liberation.

[The Dharma-gate of non-duality] The Dharma-gate of non-duality. This is the ultimate teaching that transcends relativity and differentiation. It is what, above the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates of Buddhism, can directly behold the noble path.

[Traveling everywhere through Buddha-lands, without love or weariness. Nor do they have thoughts of seeking or not seeking, nor thoughts of self and other, opposition and resentment. Why is that? Because those bodhisattvas have a mind of great compassion and benefit toward all living beings. They abandon all attachment and accomplish immeasurable merit.]

With an equal mind they travel everywhere through all Buddha-lands, saving all living beings, without love or weariness. Nor do they have thoughts of seeking or not seeking, nor thoughts of self and other, opposition and anger. Why is that? Because these bodhisattvas have a mind of great compassion and benefit toward all living beings. They abandon all attachment and accomplish immeasurable merit.

[With unobstructed wisdom, they understand dharmas as thusness. They skillfully know the arising and cessation, and the skillful means of voice and sound. They take no delight in worldly talk, but delight in right discourse. They know that all dharmas are utterly empty and still. The born body and affliction — the two remainders — are both exhausted. In the three realms they cultivate with an even mind, and reaching the One Vehicle, arrive at the other shore.]

With unobstructed wisdom (perfect and penetrating wisdom) they understand all dharmas as thusness, and skillfully expound the right Dharma (skillfully knowing arising and cessation, and the skillful means of voice and sound). They take no delight in useless worldly talk, but devote themselves to the discourses of the Great Vehicle that are ultimate and definitive (delighting in right discourse). They know that all dharmas are utterly empty and still. The bitter fruit of the born body and the residual habitual tendencies of affliction are entirely gone. In the three realms they cultivate with an even mind, thoroughly penetrating the One Vehicle teaching (the only teaching that can bring people to Buddhahood), until they reach the other shore.

[Thusness] As in true suchness. This is the self-nature state that is unmoving, still and silent, equal and non-dual, and free of inverted discrimination. [True suchness] “True” means real and not false; “thus” means unchanging as it always is. Combining the two meanings of real and not false and unchanging as it always is, it is called “true suchness,” and true suchness is the true nature of all dharmas. [Skillfully know the arising and cessation, and the skillful means of voice and sound] “Arising and cessation” refers to the four noble truths of the arising of suffering and the cessation of suffering, and “the skillful means of voice and sound” means being able to expound skillfully. [Truth] A doctrine that is true and without error.

[The four noble truths] The truth of suffering, the truth of the arising of suffering, the truth of the cessation of suffering, and the truth of the path. First, the “truth of suffering” is the truth explaining that human life is full of suffering. Suffering has the characteristic of oppression. Human life has three sufferings, eight sufferings, and immeasurable sufferings; suffering is the reality of actual human life. Second, the “arising” of the “truth of arising” means to bring about or cause; it is the truth explaining how the suffering of human life comes about. The pain of human life comes from craving, and then grasping, and then creating karma, and then undergoing suffering, and then rebirth. Third, the “truth of cessation” is the truth explaining the stilling of all suffering. When all the arising of suffering (craving) is forever cut off without remainder, with no grasping and no attachment, then there is no more creating karma, no more suffering, no more rebirth — this is the truth of cessation. Fourth, the “truth of the path” is the truth explaining how to forever cut off the arising of suffering (craving), that is, the path of ending suffering. Among the four noble truths, arising is the cause and suffering is the fruit; the path is the cause and cessation is the fruit.
[The born body]

The bodies of Buddhas and bodhisattvas are of two kinds: the Dharma body and the born body. The principle-essence they realize is called the “Dharma body,” while the flesh body born from father and mother in order to save living beings is called the “born body.” [The two remainders] The bitter fruit of the born body and the residual habitual tendencies of affliction are called the two remainders.

[Decisively cutting the net of doubt, they realize that nothing is attained. With the wisdom of skillful means, they increase their understanding. From the very beginning they dwell in spiritual powers, attain the One Vehicle path, and are awakened not through another.]

They decisively cut the net of doubt and realize the state in which in truth there is no dharma whatsoever to be attained. With the wisdom of skillful means, they increase their understanding. From the root, they dwell in spiritual powers, attain the One Vehicle path, and awaken to the Way and become Buddhas.
[Realizing that nothing is attained] This is the cutting off of the attachment to dharmas.
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
“This ignorance has no real substance; it is like a person in a dream, who is not nonexistent while dreaming, but upon waking finds nothing whatsoever.”
(For annotations see
A Detailed Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment

[Attachment to dharmas] To cling to all dharmas as truly existing; one of the two attachments (the attachment to self and the attachment to dharmas). [Attachment to self] To cling to body and mind as “I.” [The wisdom of skillful means] Also called the wisdom of expedient means, spoken in contrast to the wisdom of the real. Penetrating the true nature of all dharmas is called the wisdom of the real. Understanding the differences among all myriad phenomena is called the wisdom of expedient means (the wisdom of skillful means). [Awakened not through another] To awaken to the Way and become a Buddha not through any other path (but through the One Vehicle path).

[Their wisdom is vast and deep, like the great ocean. Their bodhi is lofty and broad, like Mount Sumeru. Their own majestic radiance surpasses the sun and moon. Their minds are white and pure, like snowy mountains. Their patience is like the earth, equal toward all. Their purity is like water, washing away all dust and defilement. Their blazing intensity is like fire, burning the fuel of affliction. Their non-attachment is like the wind, without any obstruction.]

The bodhisattvas of the Land of Ultimate Bliss have wisdom vast and deep, like the great ocean. Their bodhi-mind is lofty and broad, like Mount Sumeru. Their own majestic radiance surpasses the sun and moon. Their minds are white and pure, like snowy mountains. Their patience is like the great earth, equal toward all. Their bodies (conduct) and minds are pure like water, washing away all dust and defilement. Their wisdom is blazing like fire, cutting off affliction as fire burns fuel. Their non-attachment (non-attachment to appearances) is like the wind, without any obstruction.

[Patience like the earth] This uses the great earth as a metaphor for the patience of equality (free of all discrimination). The great earth bears all things: heavy and light, pure and filthy, it carries them alike, choosing nothing and discriminating nothing. This is used to illustrate the virtue of the bodhisattvas' patience, which is far removed from all discrimination of self and other, kindness and resentment, opposition and compliance. [Dust and defilement] A general term for affliction. [Blazing like fire, burning the fuel of affliction] Fire is a metaphor for wisdom, and firewood for affliction.

[The sound of Dharma like thunder, to awaken the unawakened. Raining the Dharma of sweet dew, to moisten living beings. Vast as empty space, because of great and equal compassion. Like a pure lotus, because it is free of defilement. Like the nyagrodha tree, because its shade is great. Like a vajra club, because it shatters wrong attachment. Like the Iron Ring Mountain, because all demons and false teachers cannot move it.]

When they expound the sutras and teach the Dharma, the sound of Dharma is like thunder, to awaken the unawakened. They rain the Dharma of sweet dew, to nourish living beings. Vast and boundless as empty space, because of great and equal compassion. Like a pure lotus, because it is free of defilement. Like the nyagrodha tree, because it shades and protects a great many living beings. Like a vajra club, because it shatters wrong attachment. Like the Iron Ring Mountain, because all demons and false teachers cannot shake it.
[The Dharma of sweet dew] The Treatise on the Stages of the Buddha Land says:

“The Tathāgata's holy teaching, among the teachings of all the false teachers and all the evil and inferior teachings of the world, is the most true. Supremely pure, it is like ghee, and like sweet dew, bringing nirvāṇa.”
[The nyagrodha tree] The Sūtra of the Retribution of Sin and Blessing says:
“The nyagrodha
tuó
tree is twenty li tall, its branches spreading in a perfect circle and covering sixty li. The seeds on the tree number tens of thousands of bushels.”

[Their minds are upright and true, skillful and decisive. In discussing the Dharma they are never satiated; in seeking the Dharma they never tire. Their precepts are like lapis lazuli, bright and pure within and without. What they say brings joy and conviction to the assembly. They beat the Dharma drum, raise the Dharma banner, shine the sun of wisdom, and shatter the darkness of delusion. Pure and gentle, still and clearly discerning. They are great guides, taming themselves and others. They lead living beings to abandon all craving and attachment, forever to leave the three defilements, and to sport in spiritual powers.]
